headline: Safe-Haven Bond Buying Pulls Rates Lower
tileReason: Worries about AI-related companies sent investors into Treasury bonds on Thursday, and the daily 30-year average fell to about 7.33% despite hot inflation data.
takeaway: Thursday's rush into bonds showed up in mortgage pricing: the daily 30-year average fell 0.12% to 7.33%, while Freddie Mac's weekly average held at 7.40%. This morning the 10-year Treasury yield is roughly where it closed Thursday, so lenders are likely to price close to yesterday. Fed Chair Warsh gave no hint of an October hike, but inflation reports keep coming in hot. Over the next month, higher, steady and lower rates look about equally likely after Thursday's drop.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Oct 28
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via ActionForex (Oct 16, 12:26 GMT); Kalshi/Polymarket via DeFi Rate (Oct 16, 7:44 AM ET) and Benzinga
fedOdds.note: CME FedWatch shows about 16%; prediction markets show 13% to 14%. Reports of Wednesday's post-CPI peak range from 44% to 54%. Polymarket still puts a December hike near 79%.

drivers.title: Investors ran to the safety of bonds
drivers.text: On Thursday, worries about heavily indebted AI-related companies spread through the tech sector, and investors moved money into U.S. Treasury bonds. More buying lifts bond prices and lowers their yields: the 10-year Treasury yield closed about 0.09% lower at 5.10%. Lenders passed the move straight through, and the daily 30-year average fell 0.12% to 7.33%.

drivers.title: Fed Chair Warsh gave no hike signal
drivers.text: Speaking at the IMF meetings in Bangkok Friday morning, Warsh said he doesn't decide meetings in advance and that the economy has broadly behaved as the Fed expected since its September hike. Traders took that as a sign October is less likely: CME FedWatch odds of an October 28 hike slipped to about 16%, from around 28% Thursday and roughly half after Wednesday's inflation report. Fewer expected hikes take some upward pressure off longer-term rates.

drivers.title: Inflation reports keep running hot
drivers.text: September wholesale prices (PPI) jumped 1.3% versus a 0.5% forecast, and this morning import prices rose 1.1% versus 0.8% expected. Rising costs for businesses and imported goods can reach store shelves later. Bond investors want higher yields when inflation looks sticky, which is why yields aren't falling further today.

drivers.title: Other Fed officials still lean toward hikes
drivers.text: Boston Fed President Susan Collins said rates may need to rise a bit further before year-end. Markets still see a December hike as likely, which keeps a floor under rates.

drivers.title: Oil stays near $106
drivers.text: Brent crude sat near $106 a barrel Friday morning, on track for a small weekly gain on Middle East supply worries. Expensive energy feeds into inflation, which leans against lower rates.

outlook.basis: I've moved to roughly even odds. Thursday's 0.12% drop already reflects the bond rally, so some of the good news is now priced in, and rallies driven by stock-market fear can fade once markets calm down. Inflation reports keep coming in hot and a December hike is still widely expected, which argues against much further improvement. On the other side, Warsh isn't pushing for an October hike, and the gap between mortgage rates and the 10-year (about 2.2% vs. a typical 2.0%) leaves room for rates to improve if that gap narrows. The October 28 Fed decision and October 29 inflation (PCE) data are the big swing events.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: Thursday's bond rally brought the daily 30-year average down to about 7.33%, below last week's 7.5% range. Inflation is still hot and the Fed meets October 28, so it's worth asking your lender how a lock, a float-down option, or a short wait would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates near 7.3% to 7.4% still stretch buyers' budgets. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to buy down their rate, can help your home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Rates dipped to about 7.33% as investors piled into bonds, but hot inflation and the Fed's October 28 meeting mean the next move could go either way.
